body:
The apparent annual movement of the overhead Sun

As Earth revolves around the Sun with its tilted axis, the latitude receiving vertically overhead sunlight at local noon changes during the year.

The point on Earth's surface where the Sun is directly overhead is called the subsolar point. At this point, the Sun's altitude above the horizon is 90°.

Over the course of a year, the latitude of the subsolar point shifts between the Tropic of Cancer at approximately 23.5° N and the Tropic of Capricorn at approximately 23.5° S.

June solstice

The June solstice occurs around 21 June. At this position in Earth's orbit, the North Pole is inclined most strongly towards the Sun.

  • The Sun is directly overhead at local noon on the Tropic of Cancer.
  • The Northern Hemisphere experiences its summer solstice.
  • The Southern Hemisphere experiences its winter solstice.
  • Most locations in the Northern Hemisphere experience their longest daylight duration of the year.
  • Most locations in the Southern Hemisphere experience their shortest daylight duration of the year.

In the ideal geographical model, the Arctic Circle marks the southern boundary of the region experiencing continuous daylight during this solstice. The Antarctic Circle marks the corresponding northern boundary of the region experiencing continuous darkness.

December solstice

The December solstice occurs around 21 or 22 December. The South Pole is then inclined most strongly towards the Sun.

  • The Sun is directly overhead at local noon on the Tropic of Capricorn.
  • The Southern Hemisphere experiences its summer solstice.
  • The Northern Hemisphere experiences its winter solstice.
  • Most locations in the Southern Hemisphere experience their longest daylight duration of the year.
  • Most locations in the Northern Hemisphere experience their shortest daylight duration of the year.

The polar illumination conditions are reversed. The Antarctic region experiences continuous daylight, while the Arctic region experiences continuous darkness.

March and September equinoxes

An equinox occurs when the Sun crosses the celestial equator, which is Earth's equator extended into the sky. At this position, the subsolar point lies on the Equator.

Neither hemisphere is tilted preferentially towards the Sun. The circle of illumination passes approximately through both geographical poles.

  • March equinox: The subsolar point crosses the Equator northward. It marks the beginning of astronomical spring in the Northern Hemisphere and autumn in the Southern Hemisphere.
  • September equinox: The subsolar point crosses the Equator southward. It marks the beginning of astronomical autumn in the Northern Hemisphere and spring in the Southern Hemisphere.

Day and night are approximately equal in duration over most of Earth during an equinox.

Approximately equal, not exactly equal

The geographical model gives about 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of darkness during an equinox. Actual daylight is generally slightly longer because the Sun has a visible disc and Earth's atmosphere bends sunlight near the horizon. Sunrise and sunset are measured using the visible upper edge of the Sun rather than its centre.

Comparison of the four seasonal positions

Conventional dateOverhead SunNorthern HemisphereSouthern Hemisphere
21 MarchEquatorSpring equinoxAutumn equinox
21 JuneTropic of CancerSummer solsticeWinter solstice
23 SeptemberEquatorAutumn equinoxSpring equinox
22 DecemberTropic of CapricornWinter solsticeSummer solstice

These conventional textbook dates are approximate. The precise astronomical events may occur on adjacent calendar dates depending on the year and time zone.

Northern and southern solstices

The June solstice is also called the northern solstice because the subsolar point reaches its northernmost latitude. The December solstice is called the southern solstice because the subsolar point reaches its southernmost latitude.

The expression summer solstice must always be understood with reference to a particular hemisphere. The same astronomical event is a summer solstice in one hemisphere and a winter solstice in the other.

Prelims focus

  • June solstice: overhead Sun at 23.5° N.
  • December solstice: overhead Sun at 23.5° S.
  • March and September equinoxes: overhead Sun at 0° latitude.
  • March equinox: northward crossing of the Equator.
  • September equinox: southward crossing of the Equator.
  • Trap: The southern solstice produces summer, not winter, in the Southern Hemisphere.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapter 3, Figure 3.3 and pp. 19-21; US Naval Observatory, The Seasons and the Earth's Orbit, Earth's Seasons, and Length of Day and Night at the Equinoxes, consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
The geographical importance of Earth's axial tilt

Earth's axial tilt determines the latitudes of the tropics and polar circles. These imaginary geographical lines mark important limits of the annual movement of the overhead Sun and the occurrence of continuous daylight and darkness.

Geographical lineLatitude
North Pole90° N
Arctic Circle66.5° N
Tropic of Cancer23.5° N
Equator0°
Tropic of Capricorn23.5° S
Antarctic Circle66.5° S
South Pole90° S

Where can the Sun be directly overhead?

The midday Sun can reach an altitude of 90° only within the region extending from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn, including both tropics. This region is known as the torrid zone or tropical zone.

  • At the Equator, the Sun is directly overhead at local noon approximately twice a year, during the equinoxes.
  • At locations strictly between the two tropics, the overhead Sun occurs approximately twice each year.
  • At the Tropic of Cancer, the overhead Sun occurs once each year, during the June solstice.
  • At the Tropic of Capricorn, the overhead Sun occurs once each year, during the December solstice.
  • Beyond the two tropics, the Sun never reaches the zenith, the point directly overhead.

Application to Gujarat

The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat, including Kutch district. Locations situated on this latitude receive vertically overhead sunlight at local solar noon around the June solstice.

At locations in Gujarat south of the Tropic of Cancer, the Sun can be directly overhead twice during the year. At locations north of the tropic, it can never be directly overhead.

When the Sun is directly overhead, a vertical object standing on level ground casts virtually no horizontal shadow. This phenomenon occurs at local solar noon rather than necessarily at 12:00 according to Indian Standard Time.

Latitudinal variation in daylight duration

The seasonal difference in day length generally increases with distance from the Equator.

The Equator experiences approximately 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of darkness throughout the year. At higher latitudes, the difference between summer and winter daylight duration becomes increasingly pronounced.

Midnight sun and polar night

The midnight sun is the phenomenon in which the Sun remains visible above the horizon even at local midnight. It occurs in polar regions during their respective summers.

Polar night is the period during which the Sun remains below the horizon throughout the daily rotation of Earth. It occurs during polar winter.

In the ideal model, the Arctic and Antarctic Circles represent the latitudinal boundaries for at least one period of approximately 24 hours of continuous daylight or darkness during the year. Actual visibility near these boundaries is influenced by atmospheric refraction and the local horizon.

Why the poles experience long periods of daylight and darkness

At the North Pole, the Sun remains above the horizon for approximately 6 months from the March equinox to the September equinox. It remains below the horizon for approximately the following 6 months.

The South Pole experiences the reverse sequence.

However, all locations within the polar circles do not experience 6 months of uninterrupted daylight or darkness. The duration generally increases towards the poles. The 6-month description applies approximately to the geographical poles themselves.

Polar night does not necessarily mean complete darkness throughout the entire period. Twilight may be present when the Sun is below but close to the horizon.

Prelims focus

  • The tropics are located at approximately 23.5° N and 23.5° S.
  • The polar circles are located at approximately 66.5° N and 66.5° S.
  • The overhead Sun never occurs outside the tropics.
  • The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat.
  • On the June solstice, the Arctic region experiences continuous daylight and the Antarctic region experiences continuous darkness.
  • Trap: Approximately 6 months of continuous daylight applies to the poles, not uniformly to the entire polar regions.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapters 2 and 3, pp. 11-12 and 19-21; US Naval Observatory, The Seasons and the Earth's Orbit and Length of Day and Night at the Equinoxes; Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, Incredible India, The Great Rann of Kutch; online references consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Daily and annual apparent solar movements

Two different apparent movements of the Sun can be observed from Earth.

The apparent daily movement of the Sun across the sky from the eastern horizon towards the western horizon is caused mainly by Earth's rotation from west to east.

The gradual annual northward and southward movement of the latitude receiving overhead sunlight is caused by Earth's axial inclination combined with its revolution around the Sun.

Annual northward and southward movement

The subsolar point moves within the tropical region throughout the year. Its northernmost limit is the Tropic of Cancer, and its southernmost limit is the Tropic of Capricorn.

Northward movement

After the December solstice, the latitude receiving overhead sunlight begins shifting northward from the Tropic of Capricorn. It crosses the Equator during the March equinox and reaches the Tropic of Cancer during the June solstice.

This apparent northward movement is astronomically associated with Uttarayan.

Southward movement

After the June solstice, the latitude receiving overhead sunlight begins shifting southward from the Tropic of Cancer. It crosses the Equator during the September equinox and reaches the Tropic of Capricorn during the December solstice.

This apparent southward movement is astronomically associated with Dakshinayan.

Changing sunrise and sunset directions

Although the Sun generally rises in the eastern part of the sky and sets in the western part, its precise points of sunrise and sunset change during the year.

For ordinary non-polar locations with an unobstructed level horizon, the following patterns apply approximately:

  • During the equinoxes, the Sun rises due east and sets due west.
  • Between the March and September equinoxes, the Sun rises north of east and sets north of west.
  • Between the September and March equinoxes, the Sun rises south of east and sets south of west.

At most locations in India, the sunrise point reaches its northernmost position around the June solstice and its southernmost position around the December solstice.

These changes are apparent movements observed from Earth's surface. They do not mean that the Sun physically revolves northward and southward around Earth.

Uttarayan in Gujarat

Gujarat celebrates the festival of Uttarayan, also known as Makar Sankranti, generally around 14 January. Kite flying is a prominent tradition associated with this festival.

The cultural festival is associated with the Sun's entry into Makara in the traditional sidereal calendar. Its calendar date must be distinguished from the astronomical turning point of the subsolar point.

The actual northward movement of the overhead Sun begins after the December solstice, around 21 or 22 December, rather than on 14 January.

Festival date and astronomical event

The traditional Uttarayan festival generally occurs around 14 January. The astronomical northward movement of the subsolar point begins around the December solstice. These are related concepts but are not identical calendar events.

Prelims focus

  • Northward movement of the subsolar point: December solstice to June solstice.
  • Southward movement of the subsolar point: June solstice to December solstice.
  • The Sun rises approximately due east and sets approximately due west on the equinoxes.
  • Gujarat's Uttarayan festival generally occurs around 14 January.
  • Trap: The Sun does not rise at exactly the same point on the eastern horizon throughout the year.

[References: NCERT, Class 8, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 17, Extended Learning, Position of the Rising Sun - Uttarayan and Dakshinayan, p. 237; NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapter 3, pp. 19-21; Gujarat Tourism, International Kite Festival, consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
The Moon's revolution around Earth

The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. It revolves around Earth in an elliptical orbit while Earth and the Moon together revolve around the Sun.

The Moon completes one revolution around Earth relative to distant stars in approximately 27.3 days. It also completes one axial rotation in approximately the same duration.

This equality between its rotation period and revolution period is called synchronous rotation. Consequently, approximately the same side of the Moon remains directed towards Earth.

The complete cycle of lunar phases, measured from one new moon to the next, lasts approximately 29.5 days. This period is called the synodic month. It is longer than the Moon's orbital period because Earth and the Moon also advance around the Sun during the interval.

Lunar phases and the illumination of the Moon

The Moon does not produce visible light of its own. It is visible primarily because its surface reflects sunlight.

Except during a lunar eclipse, approximately half of the Moon is illuminated by the Sun. As the Moon revolves around Earth, observers see different portions of this illuminated half. These changing appearances are called lunar phases.

  • New moon: The Moon lies approximately in the direction of the Sun as seen from Earth. Its illuminated hemisphere faces predominantly away from Earth.
  • Full moon: The Moon lies approximately opposite the Sun as seen from Earth. Its illuminated hemisphere faces predominantly towards Earth.

The ordinary phases of the Moon are not caused by Earth's shadow. They result from the changing relative positions of Earth, the Moon and the Sun.

Meaning of an eclipse

An eclipse occurs when a celestial body blocks the light reaching another celestial body or temporarily obstructs it from the view of an observer because of their relative alignment.

Solar and lunar eclipses involve the approximate alignment of the Sun, Earth and the Moon. A nearly straight-line arrangement of 3 celestial bodies is called a syzygy.

FeatureSolar eclipseLunar eclipse
Body in the middleMoonEarth
Required lunar phaseNew moonFull moon
Shadow cast byMoonEarth
Shadow falls onEarthMoon

Why eclipses do not occur every month

Although a new moon and a full moon occur during every lunar phase cycle, eclipses do not normally occur at every new moon or full moon.

The reason is that the plane of the Moon's orbit around Earth is inclined approximately 5.1° to the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.

The two points where the Moon's orbital path crosses Earth's orbital plane are called lunar nodes.

  • The ascending node is the point where the Moon crosses from the southern side to the northern side of Earth's orbital plane.
  • The descending node is the point where it crosses from the northern side to the southern side.

A solar eclipse can occur when a new moon takes place sufficiently close to a lunar node. A lunar eclipse can occur when a full moon takes place sufficiently close to a lunar node.

At most other new moons and full moons, the bodies do not align closely enough for the required shadow to reach its target.

Aryabhata's scientific explanation

The ancient Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata explained that Earth rotates on its axis and that the Moon and planets shine by reflected sunlight. He also gave a scientific explanation of eclipses in terms of the shadows cast by Earth and the Moon.

Prelims focus

  • The Moon's rotation and revolution periods are approximately 27.3 days.
  • The lunar phase cycle lasts approximately 29.5 days.
  • A solar eclipse requires a new moon.
  • A lunar eclipse requires a full moon.
  • The Moon's orbital plane is inclined approximately 5° to Earth's orbital plane.
  • Trap: A new moon or full moon alone is insufficient to produce an eclipse.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018-19, Chapter 1, p. 5; NCERT, Class 8, Science, 2018-19, Chapter 17, pp. 216-219 and 227; NASA, Moon Phases, Top Moon Questions, and Eclipses and the Moon, consulted 26 November 2026.]
